arXiv:2511.11733v1 [cs.DC] 13 Nov 2025

Speculative Decoding in Decentralized LLM Inference:
Turning Communication Latency into Computation Throughput

Correspondence to: tianyu@gradient.network
Abstract

Speculative decoding accelerates large language model (LLM) inference by using a lightweight draft model to propose tokens that are later verified by a stronger target model. While effective in centralized systems, its behavior in decentralized settings, where network latency often dominates compute, remains under-characterized. We present Decentralized Speculative Decoding (DSD), a plug and play framework for decentralized inference that turns communication delay into useful computation by verifying multiple candidate tokens in parallel across distributed nodes. We further introduce an adaptive speculative verification strategy that adjusts acceptance thresholds based on token level semantic importance and, in our experiments, provides up to an additional 15% to 20% end to end speedup over a nonadaptive speculative decoding baseline, without retraining. In theory, DSD reduces cross node communication cost by approximately (N−1)​t1​(k−1)/k(N-1)t_{1}(k-1)/k, where t1t_{1} is per link latency and kk is the average number of tokens accepted per round. In practice, DSD achieves up to 2.56×2.56\times speedup on HumanEval and 2.59×2.59\times on GSM8K, surpassing the Eagle3 baseline while preserving accuracy. These results show that adapting speculative decoding for decentralized execution provides a system level optimization that converts network stalls into throughput, enabling faster distributed LLM inference with no model retraining or architectural changes.

1 Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) continue to grow in size, and inference efficiency has become a critical concern for both research and production systems (Brown et al., 2020; Kaplan et al., 2020; Hoffmann et al., 2022; Narayanan et al., 2021). While modern accelerators provide increasing computational power, performance bottlenecks have shifted toward memory bandwidth and, in distributed settings, inter node communication latency (Narayanan et al., 2021; Rajbhandari et al., 2021; Shoeybi et al., 2020; Huang et al., 2019). Many existing efficiency techniques such as quantization (Dettmers et al., 2022), tensor parallelism (Shazeer et al., 2019; Rajbhandari et al., 2021), and speculative decoding (Leviathan et al., 2023) were developed for centralized or single server settings. As decentralized inference frameworks such as Parallax (Tong et al., 2025) become more common and execution spans geographically distributed nodes, communication latency can exceed per step computation time, which severely reduces the benefits of classical methods designed for centralized computation (Narayanan et al., 2021; Rajbhandari et al., 2021; Shoeybi et al., 2020). In this work we follow Parallax and use the term decentralized inference to refer to LLM serving over multiple independently managed nodes that may reside in different regions.

Speculative decoding (Leviathan et al., 2023; Miao et al., 2024) accelerates autoregressive generation by pairing a lightweight draft model with a stronger target model. The draft model predicts several candidate tokens, and the target model verifies them in a single forward pass, reducing the number of target model evaluations. Prior studies typically assume that computation dominates the total cost (Chen et al., 2023; Li et al., 2023b). In decentralized settings, however, this assumption no longer holds, because cross node communication becomes the primary overhead (Narayanan et al., 2021).

We revisit speculative decoding from a distributed systems perspective and propose Decentralized Speculative Decoding (DSD), a communication aware formulation that converts network waiting time into useful computation. Instead of leaving nodes idle during communication, DSD verifies kk tokens jointly across distributed nodes, reducing synchronization from kk rounds to a single round. For a system with NN nodes, per link latency t1t_{1}, and local compute time t0t_{0}, this reduces communication latency by approximately (N−1)​t1​(k−1)/k(N-1)t_{1}(k-1)/k. The advantage is most pronounced when 3≤N≤83\leq N\leq 8 and 3​t0<t1<10​t03t_{0}<t_{1}<10t_{0}, a regime commonly observed in wide area or mixed hardware deployments (Rajbhandari et al., 2021).

In addition, we introduce an adaptive speculative verification strategy that does not require retraining. Instead of applying the same acceptance rule to all tokens, DSD identifies high impact tokens using cross entropy contrast, token match statistics, and a distributional agreement score, and applies a relaxation factor τ\tau to adjust acceptance strength. Tokens with strong semantic influence are verified strictly, while low impact tokens are accepted more flexibly. In our experiments, this inference only mechanism provides up to an additional 15% to 20% end to end acceleration over a nonadaptive speculative decoding baseline while preserving output quality.

We implement DSD in the Parallax decentralized inference engine (Tong et al., 2025) and evaluate it on HumanEval, GSM8K, Alpaca, MT Bench, and CNN/DailyMail using Llama3.1-8B and Qwen3-8B. DSD achieves up to 2.56×\times speedup on HumanEval and 2.59×\times on GSM8K, matching or exceeding the Eagle3 baseline (Li et al., 2023b) without accuracy degradation.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    We formulate speculative decoding for decentralized inference, reducing communication frequency by verifying multiple tokens in each synchronization round without modifying model weights.

  • •

    We propose a training free adaptive verification method that adjusts token level acceptance according to semantic relevance, increasing accepted token spans while preserving accuracy.

  • •

    We provide a system level analysis that connects communication latency and verification efficiency, supported by experiments on reasoning and code generation benchmarks that show consistent acceleration at accuracy parity.

2 Methodology

We formalize DSD and describe two components: (i) speculative parallelism adapted to decentralized inference, and (ii) adaptive speculative verification that is semantically aware and training free. The objective is to increase Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) and reduce inter node latency without retraining or modifying model weights, consistent with recent system level optimization efforts (Narayanan et al., 2021; Rajbhandari et al., 2021).

2.1 Preliminaries: Standard Speculative Decoding

Speculative decoding (Leviathan et al., 2023; Miao et al., 2024) accelerates autoregressive generation by pairing a lightweight draft model MdM_{d} with a higher accuracy target model MtM_{t}. Given context x1:ix_{1:i}, the draft produces a window of γ\gamma candidate tokens

y^i+1:i+γ=Md(x1:i),\hat{y}_{i+1:i+\gamma}=M_{d}(x_{1:i}), (1)

which the target verifies in a single forward pass. Let k≤γk\leq\gamma be the number of accepted tokens. The sequence advances by appending the first kk accepted tokens and then sampling one additional token from MtM_{t}:

x1:i+k=x1:i⊕y^i+1:i+k.x_{1:i+k}=x_{1:i}\oplus\hat{y}_{i+1:i+k}. (2)

Processing a window of γ\gamma tokens at once raises effective throughput by roughly (γ+1)(\gamma+1) per target evaluation (Li et al., 2023b; Chen et al., 2023). Figure 1 illustrates how verifying a compact window shifts decoding toward a region with higher arithmetic intensity.

2.2 Decentralized Inference Model

Consider NN participating nodes, each hosting a model shard as in pipeline or tensor parallel inference systems (Shoeybi et al., 2020; Huang et al., 2019). Let t0t_{0} denote the local compute time per decoding step and t1t_{1} the point to point communication latency. With standard autoregressive decoding, producing each token requires synchronization across nodes, yielding communication overhead (N−1)​t1(N-1)t_{1} per token. The time to generate kk tokens is

Tstd=k⁡(t0+(N−1)​t1).T_{\text{std}}=k\bigl(t_{0}+(N-1)t_{1}\bigr). (3)

With decentralized speculative decoding (DSD), kk speculative tokens are verified in one synchronization round, which amortizes communication across the window:

TDSD=k​t0+(N−1)​t1.T_{\text{DSD}}=k\,t_{0}+(N-1)t_{1}. (4)

The communication reduction ratio is therefore

Rcomm=1−TDSDTstd=(N−1)​t1​(k−1)k⁡(t0+(N−1)​t1).R_{\text{comm}}=1-\frac{T_{\text{DSD}}}{T_{\text{std}}}=\frac{(N-1)t_{1}\,(k-1)}{k\bigl(t_{0}+(N-1)t_{1}\bigr)}. (5)

The benefit is most pronounced when 3≤N≤83\leq N\leq 8 and 3​t0<t1<10​t03t_{0}<t_{1}<10t_{0}, a range commonly observed in wide area or mixed hardware deployments (Tong et al., 2025). Figure 2 depicts the runtime: a draft window is verified and, if the first kk tokens pass, they are committed in a single synchronization, converting waiting into useful computation.

2.3 Adaptive Speculative Verification

Classical speculative decoding enforces strict token level distribution consistency,

Pt(yi∣x1:i−1)=Pd(yi∣x1:i−1),P_{t}(y_{i}\mid x_{1:i-1})=P_{d}(y_{i}\mid x_{1:i-1}), (6)

which ensures accuracy but can limit acceptance due to tight matching (Leviathan et al., 2023). DSD adopts adaptive verification: tokens with low semantic effect receive relaxed checks, while tokens that are expected to influence future semantics are verified rigorously.

Key token identification.

A token yiy_{i} is labeled as a key token if any of the following holds:

Key⁡(yi)⇔\displaystyle\mathrm{Key}(y_{i})\iff [Hd​(yi)Ht​(yi)>λ1]∨[|Pt(yi)−Pd(yi)|>λ2]\displaystyle\Bigl[\tfrac{H_{d}(y_{i})}{H_{t}(y_{i})}>\lambda_{1}\Bigr]\;\lor\;\Bigl[\lvert P_{t}(y_{i})-P_{d}(y_{i})\rvert>\lambda_{2}\Bigr] (7)
∨[NormMatch(yi)<λ3],\displaystyle\lor\;\Bigl[\mathrm{NormMatch}(y_{i})<\lambda_{3}\Bigr],

where HdH_{d} and HtH_{t} denote draft and target token cross entropies, and NormMatch⁡(yi)∈[0,1]\mathrm{NormMatch}(y_{i})\in[0,1] measures normalized distribution similarity between the two predictive distributions (for example based on the overlap of their top-kk support).

Thresholds λ1,λ2,λ3\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\lambda_{3} are calibrated on a small validation set.

Verification scaling.

For non key tokens, a softened target distribution is formed as

P~t​(yi)≔Pt​(yi)1−τ​Pd​(yi)τ,τ∈[0,1],\tilde{P}_{t}(y_{i})\coloneqq P_{t}(y_{i})^{1-\tau}\,P_{d}(y_{i})^{\tau},\qquad\tau\in[0,1], (8)

and then renormalized to obtain a probability distribution over the vocabulary. Acceptance is applied against P~t\tilde{P}_{t}. Key tokens always use τ=0\tau=0 for strict verification. Modest values of τ\tau extend accepted spans while preserving alignment with the target model.

2.4 Complexity and Scalability

Let ρ=k/(γ+1)\rho=k/(\gamma+1) denote the mean acceptance ratio. The expected speedup over standard decoding is

S=t0+(N−1)​t1t0/ρ+(N−1)​t1/k.S=\frac{t_{0}+(N-1)t_{1}}{t_{0}/\rho+(N-1)t_{1}/k}. (9)

DSD improves end to end throughput through two complementary effects: longer accepted spans increase compute utilization, and amortized synchronization reduces communication cost. In practice, γ\gamma is set to balance arithmetic intensity and acceptance stability, and τ\tau is chosen in a modest range (for example 0.10.1 to 0.30.3) to extend acceptance without harming accuracy (Li et al., 2023b). The additional statistics for adaptive verification (cross entropies and NormMatch) are computed from logits and add only a small constant factor overhead on top of standard decoding. These settings allow DSD to maintain consistent quality while scaling to distributed and cross region clusters.

3 Experiments

We evaluate DSD across multiple model sizes, datasets, and deployment settings. The analysis focuses on three questions: (i) how much acceleration DSD achieves relative to centralized speculative decoding and strong systems such as Eagle3 (Li et al., 2023b), (ii) whether adaptive verification maintains accuracy across varied benchmarks, and (iii) how performance changes as the accepted span kk and the relaxation coefficient τ\tau vary.

3.1 Experimental Setup

Models. We use two open weight models, Llama3.1-8B (Grattafiori et al., 2024) and Qwen3-8B (Bai et al., 2023). Both are deployed in the Parallax decentralized inference engine (Tong et al., 2025). Each replica spans four to eight nodes. Each node has one NVIDIA A800 (80 GB) and a 100 Gbps InfiniBand link, consistent with recent distributed LLM systems (Narayanan et al., 2021; Rajbhandari et al., 2021).

Datasets. We evaluate five representative tasks: HumanEval (Chen et al., 2021) for code generation (pass@kk), GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021) for mathematical reasoning (exact match), AlpacaEval (Li et al., 2023a) for instruction following (win rate), MT Bench (Zheng et al., 2023) for multi turn dialogue (score or win rate), and CNN/DailyMail (Nallapati et al., 2016) for summarization (ROUGE-L).

Systems compared. We compare three inference strategies. Baseline uses standard autoregressive decoding without speculative steps. Eagle3 is a strong centralized speculative framework with tight draft–target agreement (Li et al., 2023b). DSD introduces decentralized speculative decoding with adaptive token verification, enabling synchronized multi node execution with relaxed checks for low impact tokens while keeping strict checks for semantically important positions.

Metrics. We report (i) task accuracy per dataset definition, (ii) acceleration rate over the baseline, (iii) average accepted length per verification round, and when applicable, (iv) token throughput and (v) communication reduction, following standard practice for speculative decoding (Leviathan et al., 2023; Miao et al., 2024).

Hyperparameters. Unless noted, we use a draft window γ=8\gamma=8, temperature T=1.0T=1.0, top kk sampling with k=1k=1, and relaxation τ∈[0.1,0.3]\tau\in[0.1,0.3]. Each configuration is run three times with different seeds. Decoding batch size is 11, and the maximum number of new tokens follows dataset conventions. In Table 1, the Variable column uses tt for temperature, kk for the pass@kk setting, q​xqx for the draft quantization configuration, rr for the adaptive relaxation parameter, and dd for the injected latency used in the system level scaling experiment.

3.2 Results

Quantitative results. Table 1 summarizes the main outcomes. DSD consistently accelerates inference over Eagle3 while maintaining comparable or higher accuracy across models and tasks. On HumanEval and GSM8K, the best DSD configurations reach up to 2.56×2.56\times and 2.59×2.59\times speedup respectively relative to the baseline.

Cross dataset comparison. Table 2 reports AlpacaEval, MT Bench, and CNN/DailyMail. Across all tasks, DSD improves both acceleration and average accepted length over Eagle3 (Li et al., 2023b) while maintaining comparable output quality.

Ablation: effect of the relaxation coefficient τ\tau. Varying τ\tau from 0.00.0 to 0.80.8 shows a clear speed versus accuracy trade off, consistent with prior work (Leviathan et al., 2023; Li et al., 2023b; Miao et al., 2024). Acceleration increases steadily and reaches about 2.6×2.6\times, while accuracy loss remains small in the range τ∈[0.1,0.3]\tau\in[0.1,0.3] that we use by default. In this range, adaptive verification provides additional speedup on top of nonadaptive speculative decoding while keeping accuracy within the variance of the baseline.

Ablation: impact of node scaling. We simulate deployments with two to sixteen nodes, consistent with prior distributed inference studies (Narayanan et al., 2021; Rajbhandari et al., 2021). Communication amortization keeps total latency growth sublinear. At eight nodes, DSD reduces communication cost by about 37%37\% relative to standard speculative decoding (Leviathan et al., 2023), confirming that multi token verification mitigates cross node overhead.

Qualitative analysis. Adaptive verification increases selectivity on high impact tokens such as function names, numeric values, and key control symbols, while relaxing acceptance for punctuation and filler tokens. This behavior aligns with token importance observations in recent post training and editing studies (Zheng et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2021). Outputs remain coherent and semantically stable, and in multi turn dialogue settings the acceptance gain nearly doubles throughput with no observed loss of fluency.

Summary. DSD provides up to about 2.6×\times acceleration and about 37% communication reduction while maintaining accuracy on HumanEval (Chen et al., 2021) and GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021). Gains hold up to eight nodes, showing that DSD converts communication delay into useful computation and enables efficient decentralized inference without model modification (Tong et al., 2025).

4 Conclusion

We presented DSD, a communication aware speculative decoding framework for large scale distributed inference. DSD turns network delay into useful computation by verifying multiple tokens in a single synchronization and by applying a semantically aware, training free acceptance rule. The method couples speculative parallelism, which reduces synchronization from kk rounds to one per kk tokens, with adaptive verification that gives strict checks to key tokens and relaxed checks to low impact tokens via a coefficient τ\tau, yielding up to an additional 15% to 20% end to end speedup over nonadaptive speculative decoding without retraining. Experiments on HumanEval, GSM8K, AlpacaEval, MT Bench, and CNN/DailyMail show up to 2.56×2.56\times acceleration with slight accuracy gains and up to 2.59×2.59\times at accuracy parity, outperforming strong centralized baselines such as Eagle3 and scaling smoothly with node count and draft length. DSD is most effective when link latency is several multiples of local compute and the number of nodes is moderate, a setting common in wide area or heterogeneous clusters. Beyond performance, DSD supports decentralized and privacy preserving inference, with relevance to federated and community driven compute. Future work includes asynchronous execution to reduce stragglers, heterogeneous draft cascades, integration with quantization and MoE systems, and refined analysis of how to convert latency into throughput.
